question_text: Faster economic growth requires increased share of the manufacturing sector in GDP, particularly of MSMEs. Comment on the present policies of the Government in this regard. (Answer in 150 words)
topic: Manufacturing, MSMEs and current policy
topics: Manufacturing, MSMEs and current policy
keyPointers: A services-heavy GDP grows without employing enough hands
MSMEs are the employment side of manufacturing
Credit, a definition, and a production-linked incentive are the present tools
Policy helps the firm that can comply, and misses the firm that cannot

points.text: India's growth has been light on factories, and the missing factories are mostly small.
Present policy raises a credit guarantee, redefines the MSME, and uses production-linked incentives to pull investment into chosen sectors.
Delayed payments, a compliance burden and a thin link to a large buyer still keep the small firm out of the manufacturing share.
The direction is right. The share will rise only if the policy reaches the firm that is too small to hire a consultant.

question_text: What is the status of digitalization in the Indian economy? Examine the problems faced in this regard and suggest improvements. (Answer in 150 words)
topic: Digitalisation of the Indian economy
topics: Digitalisation of the Indian economy
keyPointers: Payments and identity are digitised; the small firm often is not
The problem is access, trust and a process that still wants paper
A digital economy excludes the person who cannot stay online
Improvement is literacy, a grievance and an open system, not another app

points.text: India has digitised payments and identity faster than it has digitised the ordinary enterprise.
UPI, Aadhaar and a growing stack of public platforms are the achievement. A kirana's accounts, a land record and a small factory's compliance are the lag.
Fraud, a language barrier, patchy connectivity and departments that do not share data are the problems.
The improvement is a simpler interface, a real remedy for a failed transaction, and a rule that a digital proof is accepted the first time.

question_text: How does e-Technology help farmers in production and marketing of agricultural produce? Explain it. (Answer in 150 words)
topic: E-technology in farm production and marketing
topics: E-technology in farm production and marketing
keyPointers: The tool helps twice: in the field and in the price
Advisories, sensors and a soil test raise the decision, not the land
A platform lets the farmer see a mandi before he hires the truck
Technology fails where the phone, the road or the payment does

points.text: E-technology helps the farmer by replacing a guess with a piece of information, in the field and at the market.
Weather, pest and nutrient advisories, and a cheap sensor, change what is sown and when it is sprayed.
Electronic trading, a direct platform and a digital payment let him compare a price and get the money without the whole chain taking a cut.
The help is real for the farmer who is online and near a road. For the others it is still a scheme.

question_text: State the objectives and measures of land reforms in India. Discuss how land ceiling policy on landholding can be considered as an effective reform under economic criteria. (Answer in 150 words)
topic: Land reforms and the economic case for a ceiling
topics: Land reforms and the economic case for a ceiling
keyPointers: The objective was to end a tenure that did not farm and to give the tiller a stake
Abolition of intermediaries, a tenancy law and a ceiling were the measures
A ceiling is economic if the surplus land produces more in small hands
It failed economically where the surplus was hidden or too poor to farm

points.text: Land reform aimed to remove the intermediary and to put a ceiling on what one household could hold.
The measures were abolition of zamindari, regulation of rent, security of tenure, and a ceiling with redistribution of the surplus.
Under an economic test the ceiling works if the small owner invests more labour per acre than the absentee large owner did, and the evidence often said yes.
It is an effective reform where the surplus was real and the new owner got credit. A paper ceiling that left the land with the old owner was not.

question_text: Introduce the concept of Artificial Intelligence (AI). How does AI help clinical diagnosis? Do you perceive any threat to privacy of the individual in the use of AI in healthcare? (Answer in 150 words)
topic: AI in clinical diagnosis and the privacy risk
topics: AI in clinical diagnosis and the privacy risk
keyPointers: AI is a system that finds a pattern a rule was not written to find
In diagnosis it reads an image or a record faster than a tired eye
The help is a second opinion, not a replacement of the clinician
The health record is the privacy, and a model trained on it can leak the person

points.text: Artificial intelligence is software that learns a pattern from examples and then applies it to a new case.
In the clinic it flags a lesion on a scan, ranks a likely diagnosis and notices a combination a single doctor may miss.
The threat is real. A record, a face and a genome, once used to train a model, can identify the patient far outside the hospital.
The use is justified with consent, a limit on reuse, and a doctor who remains responsible for the decision.

question_text: Discuss several ways in which microorganisms can help in meeting the current fuel shortage. (Answer in 150 words)
topic: Microorganisms and the fuel shortage
topics: Microorganisms and the fuel shortage
keyPointers: A microbe can turn waste into a gas or a liquid fuel
Ethanol, biogas, hydrogen and a microbial fuel cell are the routes
The help is a supplement, not a replacement of the barrel
The limit is feedstock, land and a process that still costs more than oil

points.text: Some microorganisms already do, slowly, what a refinery does: they turn organic matter into a fuel.
Yeast makes ethanol, bacteria make biogas and biobutanol, and algae and engineered microbes can yield a biodiesel or a hydrogen.
A microbial fuel cell can draw electricity from waste water. Agricultural residue is the feedstock that does not need a new field.
They help by using a waste we already have. They do not, at present scale, close the shortage by themselves.

question_text: Dam failures are always catastrophic, especially on the downstream side, resulting in a colossal loss of life and property. Analyze the various causes of dam failures. Give two examples of large dam failures. (Answer in 150 words)
topic: Causes and examples of dam failure
topics: Causes and examples of dam failure
keyPointers: A dam fails by overtopping, a weak foundation, or a gate that does not open
Age, silt and a flood larger than the design are the usual partners
The downstream death is a failure of warning as well as of concrete
Two large failures are enough to show the pattern

points.text: A dam fails when the water it was built to hold finds a way over, through or under it.
Overtopping in a flood, internal erosion or piping, a foundation that settles, an earthquake, and a spillway or gate that jams are the main causes. Silt reduces the flood cushion.
The Machhu II failure in Gujarat in 1979 and the collapse of the Derna dams in Libya in 2023 each killed on a large scale downstream. The Banqiao failure in China in 1975 is the other classic.
The catastrophe is largest where a siren, a cleared spillway and a practised downstream evacuation were missing.

question_text: What is oil pollution? What are its impacts on the marine ecosystem? In what way is oil pollution particularly harmful for a country like India? (Answer in 150 words)
topic: Oil pollution and why it hits India harder
topics: Oil pollution and why it hits India harder
keyPointers: Oil pollution is petroleum entering a water the ecosystem has to live in
It smothers, poisons and persists on a shore and in a food chain
India is exposed because its sea is a highway and a fishery
A long coast and a poor fishing village make the same spill unequal

points.text: Oil pollution is the release of crude oil or a refined fuel into the sea, from a tanker, a well, a pipeline or a routine discharge.
It coats birds and mangroves, kills eggs and larvae, and enters the fish that people eat. A slick also blocks the light and the oxygen a coastal water needs.
India's harm is sharper because a huge share of its trade and fuel moves by sea, and millions depend on a coastal fishery and a mangrove that a spill ruins for years.
For India the damage is ecological and it is the next season's income of the fishing village.

question_text: Winning of 'Hearts and Minds' in terrorism-affected areas is an essential step in restoring the trust of the population. Discuss the measures adopted by the Government in this respect as part of the conflict resolution in Jammu and Kashmir. (Answer in 150 words)
topic: Hearts and minds in Jammu and Kashmir
topics: Hearts and minds in Jammu and Kashmir
keyPointers: Force without trust refills the recruitment the force just reduced
The measures mix a civic gesture, a job and a surrender policy
Operation Sadbhavana is the name most often attached to the approach
Trust is won by a predictable administration, not by a camp alone

points.text: In a terrorism-affected place the population is the ground both sides are fighting for.
In Jammu and Kashmir the government and the Army have used civic action, schools, health camps and a surrender-and-rehabilitation route alongside the security grid.
Restoration of a political process, jobs for local youth and compensation for a civilian harm are the measures that speak to trust rather than to a patrol.
Hearts and minds is essential, and it fails if the civic camp is followed by an abuse the camp cannot explain.

question_text: The use of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) by our adversaries across the borders to ferry arms/ammunitions, drugs, etc., is a serious threat to the internal security. Comment on the measures being taken to tackle this threat. (Answer in 150 words)
topic: Cross-border drones and the response
topics: Cross-border drones and the response
keyPointers: A small drone carries a payload under the old radar picture
The threat is arms and drugs delivered without a crossing party
Detection, a physical fence and a new offence are the measures
The cheap drone will keep ahead of a slow procurement

points.text: A drone lets an adversary deliver a rifle or a packet of heroin without sending a person across the fence.
The measures are anti-drone systems on the western border, better surveillance, a legal ban on a rogue flight, and joint action by the border force and the police who receive the drop.
Seizures have risen, which shows both the effort and the scale of the attempt.
The threat is serious because the device is cheap. The answer has to be a standing detection grid, not a purchase after each incident.

question_text: Most of the unemployment in India is structural in nature. Examine the methodology adopted to compute unemployment in the country and suggest improvements. (Answer in 250 words)
topic: Structural unemployment and how India counts it
topics: Structural unemployment and how India counts it
keyPointers: Structural unemployment is a mismatch of skill and place, not a lack of any work
The usual status, the weekly status and the daily status count different things
A low usual-status rate can hide a person who worked too little
The method should show underemployment and a skill mismatch, not only a zero

points.text: If most Indian unemployment is structural, a single rate of people with no work at all will misread it.
The Periodic Labour Force Survey uses usual status over a year, current weekly status, and current daily status. Each answers a different question about who is without work.
Usual status treats a person with some work in the year as employed, so a seasonal and a disguised unemployment disappear. The daily status catches more of the gap and is used less in the headline.
The method also says little about whether the unemployed person's skill matches the vacancy, which is the structural point.
The improvement is to publish the daily and the underemployment figures beside the usual rate, and to add a measure of skill and location mismatch.

question_text: Distinguish between 'care economy' and 'monetized economy'. How can care economy be brought into monetized economy through women empowerment? (Answer in 250 words)
topic: Care economy, the monetised economy and women
topics: Care economy, the monetised economy and women
keyPointers: Care is the unpaid work that makes the paid economy possible
The monetised economy counts only what is sold
Women carry the care, so their paid work stays partial
Bringing care in means paying, sharing and counting it

points.text: The care economy is the cooking, cleaning, childcare and nursing that is done without a wage. The monetised economy is the work a market pays for.
One produces people who can go to a job. The other produces the GDP. National accounts have long counted only the second.
Because women do most of the care, they enter the monetised economy late, part-time, or not at all.
Empowerment brings care across by a crèche, a paid caregiver, a man's share of the housework, and a statistic that records the unpaid hours as work.
The shift is not to put a price on affection. It is to stop treating women's time as a free input.

question_text: Explain the changes in cropping pattern in India in the context of changes in consumption pattern and marketing conditions. (Answer in 250 words)
topic: Cropping pattern, consumption and markets
topics: Cropping pattern, consumption and markets
keyPointers: Farmers grow what is eaten and what the market will buy
Cereals still dominate where procurement is certain
Diet has moved toward vegetables, milk, fruit and a protein
Marketing, a cold chain and a price decide whether the diet is planted

points.text: India's cropping pattern has followed two masters: a public buyer of grain, and a consumer who now eats more than grain.
Rice and wheat expanded where irrigation and a guaranteed procurement made them the safe crop, even in places that once grew millets and pulses.
Rising income shifted consumption toward horticulture, milk, eggs and edible oil, and the area under fruit, vegetable and a commercial crop followed where a market existed.
A weak cold chain, a distant mandi and an import of oil and pulse kept some of that shift from becoming a stable pattern.
The pattern changes when the consumer changes and the market can carry the new crop. Procurement still freezes a large part of it in two cereals.

question_text: What are the direct and indirect subsidies provided to farm sector in India? Discuss the issues raised by the World Trade Organization (WTO) in relation to agricultural subsidies. (Answer in 250 words)
topic: Farm subsidies and the WTO dispute
topics: Farm subsidies and the WTO dispute
keyPointers: A direct subsidy pays the farmer or cuts his price
An indirect subsidy cheapens power, water, fertiliser or credit
The WTO argument is that some of this support distorts trade
India's reply is that the support is for food and for a small farmer, and the method of counting is unfair

points.text: India supports farming both by paying the farmer and by cheapening what he uses.

Direct support includes a minimum support price with procurement, a cash income transfer, and a premium on crop insurance. Indirect support includes subsidised fertiliser, power, canal water and a cheap credit.
At the WTO other members argue that price support and input subsidies exceed the limit allowed for trade-distorting support, and that public stockholding for food security can push exports.
India argues that the ceiling uses an old reference price, that most farmers are low-income, and that holding a public stock is not an export subsidy.
The issue is a real disagreement about what a developing country may do to keep food and a small farm standing.

question_text: The adoption of electric vehicles is rapidly growing worldwide. How do electric vehicles contribute to reducing carbon emissions and what are the key benefits they offer compared to traditional combustion engine vehicles? (Answer in 250 words)
topic: Electric vehicles, carbon and the comparison with combustion engines
topics: Electric vehicles, carbon and the comparison with combustion engines
keyPointers: The tailpipe emission moves to the power plant
The carbon falls only if the electricity is cleaner than the fuel
The other benefits are local air, noise, efficiency and a cheaper running cost
The new costs are the battery, the mineral and the grid

points.text: An electric vehicle cuts carbon by burning no fuel on the road and by using a motor that wastes less of its energy.
The emission then depends on how the electricity was made. A coal-heavy grid reduces the gain. A cleaner grid, and a lifetime count that includes making the battery, is the honest comparison.
Against a combustion engine the benefits are no exhaust in the city, less noise, fewer moving parts, and a lower cost per kilometre.
The vehicle also needs a charge point, a grid that can take the load, and a plan for a battery that will one day be waste.
The contribution is real and it is not automatic. It is as clean as the power and as durable as the system built around the car.

question_text: What is the main task of India's third moon mission which could not be achieved in its earlier mission? List the countries that have achieved this task. Introduce the subsystems in the spacecraft launched and explain the role of the Virtual Launch Control Centre at the Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre which contributed to the successful launch from Sriharikota. (Answer in 250 words)
topic: Chandrayaan-3 and the soft landing
topics: Chandrayaan-3 and the soft landing
keyPointers: The unfinished task was a soft landing on the Moon
The United States, the Soviet Union and China had done it before India
The craft was a propulsion module, a lander and a rover
A virtual control centre let the launch be run with a dispersed team

points.text: Chandrayaan-3's main task was a soft landing, which Chandrayaan-2 had attempted and lost in the last minutes.
Before India, the United States, the erstwhile Soviet Union and China had soft-landed on the Moon. India became the fourth, and the first to land near the south pole.

The spacecraft had a propulsion module that carried it from Earth orbit toward the Moon, the Vikram lander that made the descent, and the Pragyan rover that moved on the surface. Navigation, propulsion, a hazard camera and the landing legs were the lander's critical subsystems.

The Virtual Launch Control Centre at the Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre let engineers monitor and clear the launch from Sriharikota without all of them being in one room, which mattered for a campaign run under distancing rules.
The mission finished the one task the previous attempt had left open, with a simpler lander and a control room that no longer had to be a single hall.

question_text: Comment on the National Wetland Conservation Programme initiated by the Government of India and name a few India's wetlands of international importance included in the Ramsar Sites. (Answer in 250 words)
topic: Wetland conservation and India's Ramsar sites
topics: Wetland conservation and India's Ramsar sites
keyPointers: The programme treated wetlands as a site to be funded, not as waste land
It later folded into a wider wetland rules regime
A Ramsar listing is a status, not by itself a guard
A few sites show how wide the list has become

points.text: The National Wetland Conservation Programme was India's early attempt to stop treating marshes as land waiting to be drained.
It identified wetlands, funded their management with the states, and later sat alongside the wetland rules and a national plan that made encroachment and a prohibited activity explicit.

Ramsar listing adds an international status. Chilika, Keoladeo, Loktak, Wular, Sambhar, Ashtamudi and the Sundarbans wetland are among India's sites of international importance. The list has since grown to cover many more.
The comment has a limit. A programme and a plaque do not stop sewage, a real-estate fill or a weed if the state does not enforce the boundary.
The programme mattered because it named the wetland as a public asset. Its success is the boundary that is still wet.

question_text: The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) has predicted a global sea level rise of about one metre by AD 2100. What would be its impact in India and the other countries in the Indian Ocean region? (Answer in 250 words)
topic: A one-metre sea level rise in the Indian Ocean
topics: A one-metre sea level rise in the Indian Ocean
subTopics: Sea level rise in the Indian Ocean
keyPointers: A metre of sea is a lost shore, not only a higher tide
India's deltas, islands and a west-coast city are the exposed edge
Neighbours with a low island or a crowded delta have less room to retreat
The impact is salt, a storm surge and a displaced people

points.text: A global rise of about a metre by 2100 would redraw the Indian Ocean's inhabited edge.

In India the Sundarbans, the Mahanadi and Godavari deltas, low stretches of Kerala and Mumbai, and the islands of Lakshadweep would face permanent inundation, salt in the field and a higher storm surge.
Bangladesh, the Maldives, Sri Lanka's low coast and parts of island Southeast Asia and East Africa share the same sea and have fewer inland places to move a population.
Ports, a coastal fishery and a groundwater that turns saline are the economic impact. Migration is the social one.
The region does not have to wait for 2100. The same rise, arriving as a surge on top of a higher base, is already a planning fact.

question_text: What are the internal security challenges being faced by India? Give out the role of Central Intelligence and Investigative Agencies tasked to counter such threats. (Answer in 250 words)
topic: Internal security challenges and the central agencies
topics: Internal security challenges and the central agencies
keyPointers: The challenges are terror, a cross-border proxy, insurgency, cyber and a communal riot
No single agency holds all of them
Intelligence warns; investigation builds the case
The weakness is the seam between the collector of the warning and the force that must act

points.text: India's internal security problems are several campaigns at once, not one enemy.
Cross-border terrorism, a residual insurgency, Left-wing extremism, a communal and a caste violence, organised crime, drugs, a drone drop and a cyber attack on infrastructure are the present list.

The Intelligence Bureau collects and warns inside the country. The Research and Analysis Wing watches the external source. The National Investigation Agency takes the terror case. The Narcotics Control Bureau, the National Technical Research Organisation and a cyber agency cover the specialist threats.
State police still make the arrest. A central agency that does not share in time leaves the local force blind.
The role of the agencies is warning, a lawful case and a shared picture. The challenge is largest where that picture arrives late.

question_text: Give out the major sources of terror funding in India and the efforts being made to curtail these sources. In the light of this, also discuss the aim and objective of the No Money for Terror (NMFT) Conference recently held at New Delhi in November 2022. (Answer in 250 words)
topic: Terror funding and the No Money for Terror conference
topics: Terror funding and the No Money for Terror conference
keyPointers: The money comes from a state proxy, a fake charity, crime and a hawala route
Cutting it means the bank, the charity and the cash route, not only the gunman
India has laws and a financial intelligence unit aimed at the flow
NMFT was a meeting to make that cutoff a shared international practice

points.text: Terror in India is funded by a mix of outside money, criminal profit and a charity that is not what it says.
The sources include a foreign state or diaspora channel, fake non-governmental organisations, extortion, drugs, counterfeit currency, hawala and the misuse of a crypto transfer.
The efforts are the Unlawful Activities law, a ban and a seizure, the Financial Intelligence Unit, tighter rules on a non-profit, and action against fake currency and a hawala operator.

The No Money for Terror conference in New Delhi in November 2022 aimed to build a common political will, to share the methods of tracing a fund, and to close the gaps a single country's law cannot reach.
The objective is simple to state and hard to finish: a terrorist group should find that the money stops before the weapon does.
